extracted.intended_audience: poets, aspiring poets, and writers (especially those seeking patronage) interested in craft and literary conduct
extracted.subtask_description: Advice and evaluative criteria for composing poetry and managing relations with patrons, drawn from Horace's epistles (craft, originality, audience, performance vs. reader, and professional conduct).

rubrics_metrics.name: Originality — avoid slavish imitation
rubrics_metrics.description: Be the originator rather than a mere imitator: 'I was the original, who set my free footsteps upon the vacant sod... He who depends upon himself, as leader, commands the swarm.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Imitation of another's faults or servile copying deceives the ignorant and provokes ridicule; strive for individual voice and leadership rather than copying existing poets wholesale.

rubrics_metrics.name: Imitate measures/metrics, not subject or manner
rubrics_metrics.description: Follow the numbers and spirit of admired models (e.g., Archilochus) but not their subject and style: 'following the numbers and spirit of Archilochus, but not his subject and style.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Adopt metrical forms or technical strengths from predecessors while changing subjects, tone, and stylistic manner so as to avoid unoriginal lampooning or slavish mimicry (examples: Sappho, Alcaeus).

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not pander to the inconstant vulgar
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid writing merely to please the fickle masses or court popular applause: 'I hunt not after the applause of the inconstant vulgar... I am not an auditor of noble writers, nor a vindictive reciter, nor condescend to court the tribes and desks of the grammarians.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Resist producing work that flatters popular taste at the expense of artistic integrity (e.g., relying on spectacle or pandering jests). Quality should not be sacrificed for transient popularity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Select medium and audience deliberately (reader vs. spectator)
rubrics_metrics.description: Know whether you write for private readers or for public performance: 'who had rather trust themselves with a reader, than bear the disdain of a haughty spectator... that poet to me seems able to walk upon an extended rope, who with his fictions grieves my soul...'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If you prefer the reflective reader, shape work for reading; if you aim for theatre, prepare for public scrutiny and the requirements of performance (voice, stagecraft, clarity under noise).

rubrics_metrics.name: Comedy is deceptively laborious
rubrics_metrics.description: Comedy appears easy but requires great care: 'Comedy is believed to require the least pains... the less indulgence it meets with, the more labor it requires.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not underestimate comic writing; create believable characters, precise timing, and carefully crafted situations (examples: Plautus' skill in character and comic devices).

rubrics_metrics.name: Choose subjects within your capacity
rubrics_metrics.description: Pick subjects suited to your strength and avoid grand themes you cannot sustain: 'neither does your majesty admit of humble poetry, nor dares my modesty attempt a subject which my strength is unable to support.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ambition should be tempered by honest assessment of skill; attempt loftier topics only if you can adequately handle their demands in style, scope, and learning.

rubrics_metrics.name: Present work only when fit (mental/physical condition)
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid offering or performing work when thoughtful, fatigued, pained, or distracted: 'we poets... often do ourselves many mischiefs, when we present a work to you while thoughtful or fatigued... when we are pained, if my friend has dared to find fault with one line; when, unasked, we read over again passages already repeated.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Polish and present work at proper moments; do not force incomplete or emotionally compromised pieces on patrons or audiences; avoid repetitive self-exposure and unnecessary readings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Power to move the audience as a primary test of skill
rubrics_metrics.description: A poet's excellence is shown by the ability to affect emotions: 'that poet to me seems able to walk upon an extended rope, who with his fictions grieves my soul, enrages, soothes, fills it with false terrors.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate poetry by its capacity to provoke, comfort, terrify, or move — technical virtuosity should serve emotional effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not let isolated brilliant lines mask overall weakness
rubrics_metrics.description: A bright expression should not be allowed to carry an otherwise poor work: 'if by chance a bright expression shines forth, and if one line or two [happen to be] somewhat terse and musical, this unreasonably carries off and sells the whole poem.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Judge a work by its overall coherence and sustained quality rather than a few striking phrases; avoid relying on isolated epigrams to redeem a weak poem.

rubrics_metrics.name: Antiquity is not an automatic mark of excellence
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not valorize a work solely because it is old: 'If, because the most ancient writings of the Greeks are also the best, Roman authors are to be weighed in the same scale...' and a suggestion that age alone should not determine merit.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess poems on intrinsic quality rather than age or mere survival; avoid uncritical reverence for antiquity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Poetry's pedagogical and moral role
rubrics_metrics.description: Poets instruct and form character: 'The poet fashions the child's tender and lisping mouth... he records virtuous actions, he instructs the rising age with approved examples, he comforts the indigent and the sick.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be mindful that poetry can shape morals and manners; consider ethical and educative impacts when composing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid obsequious flattery; maintain sincerity with patrons
rubrics_metrics.description: Beware imitating a flatterer; virtue lies between flattery and bluntness: 'you will beware of imitating a flatterer, while you profess yourself a friend... Virtue is the medium of the two vices.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cultivate patrons with modesty and honesty rather than sycophancy; be friendly but not toad-eating or grotesquely blunt — aim for balanced sincerity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be discreet and keep confidences
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not pry into secrets nor spread what is entrusted: 'Do not you at any time pry into his secrets, and keep close what is intrusted to you... Avoid an inquisitive impertinent, for such a one is also a tattler... a word, once sent abroad, flies irrevocably.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Professional reputation depends on discretion; avoid loose talk that damages relationships and patron trust.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cultivate patrons tactfully; avoid public whining for favors
rubrics_metrics.description: Behave modestly in asking favors and do not complain of poverty to your patron: 'Those who mention nothing of their poverty before their lord, will gain more than the importunate... A crow that could have fed in silence would have had better fare.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Seek patronage through measured respect and tact rather than immoderate entreaties or public lament; modest acceptance often secures more than importunity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Vet and recommend persons carefully
rubrics_metrics.description: Before recommending someone to a patron, check their merits: 'Look over and over again [into the merits of] such a one, as you recommend; lest afterward the faults of others strike you with shame... once deceived, forbear to defend one who suffers by his own bad conduct.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Protect your reputation by only endorsing people you have verified; defend the truly known but avoid excusing those proven unworthy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Adapt public manners to preserve favor
rubrics_metrics.description: Yield in minor matters to a patron's tastes and present yourself agreeably in their company: 'so do you yield to the gentle dictates of your friend in power... arise and lay aside the peevishness of your unmannerly muse, that you may sup together on the delicious fare purchased by your labor.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Small concessions in manners and behavior to suit a patron's leisure or tastes (e.g., joining their amusements) preserve relations and opportunities; balance independence with diplomacy.
